Sysadmin deployed Gitea as a Git server for a small project with 8 users. Much simpler than a full GitLab instance: one binary and that's it. Users were instantly familiar with the GitHub-like interface, and non-contributors read source through the web UI instead of cloning.

Devops sysadmin wishes they had picked Gogs/Gitea over GitLab. Their GitLab install uses 4 cores and 8GB RAM, and its backup rake task has triggered the OOM killer 3 times. Says Gitea is massively less resource hungry.

Runs Gitea on a $5 VPS for all personal projects and says it works great, good enough for maybe 80% of use cases. Accesses the UI only via SSH port forwarding because they're unsure how secure it is when exposed publicly. Wishes it had a GitHub Pages–like feature for project docs.
After browsing the Gitea test instance, felt it has open-source UX issues (CSS, spacing, design, typefaces) that make it somewhat grating to use.

Uses Gitea (previously Gogs) for a team of 45 with a very pleasant experience. Docker setup was smooth and it works easily with Certbot. Downside: lacks good documentation, though Gogs' docs can fill the gap.
Called it a painless installation that other self-hosted projects should imitate. Had skipped Discourse, Mastodon and GitLab because they were a pain to set up on a base Linux system.
Has used Gitea + Drone for several years and couldn't be happier: stable, fast, and it just works without consuming lots of RAM.
Uses Gitea as an OIDC identity provider, making it the linchpin for SSO across a set of developer services.
Last time they tried Gitea, migrating existing git repos was surprisingly difficult.
4+ years of use with no complaints, and it keeps getting better. Upgrades are super simple: stop the service, replace the single binary, start it again.

Startup uses Gitea and finds issues: migrations go up but not down, a nonstandard web framework (go-macaron), too much logic in Go templates, and strange error reporting. Notes much of this was inherited from Gogs.
Uses the repo mirroring feature to keep local copies of followed projects, which saved them when authors deleted repos. Runs Gitea from a USB stick and as a Tor hidden service.
Migrated the TiDB repo to the 'Try Gitea' service. The Activity tab with a 1-year period took nearly 90s to load, and there seemed to be no caching: reloading was just as slow.
Fine for a one-person show or small company, but once you get bigger you hit various issues often and wish for GitHub again.
Sorely misses subscription/watch management, like listing and filtering what you're watching as on GitHub. Also no user-facing session management.

A previous company self-hosted Gitea without a dedicated DevOps person, so engineers spent extra time on maintenance. During a SOC-2 audit, SaaS hosting would have been easier than screenshotting everything for auditors.

Moved from self-hosted GitLab to Gitea + Nexus + Drone because keeping GitLab updated was a burden. Finds GitHub/GitLab's UI (org navigation) somewhat better, but on 4GB RAM Gitea was snappy where GitLab was laggy. Drone is less capable than GitLab CI.
Grateful for Gitea: it performs well on slow hardware (a fitlet2 with an Atom x7-E3950), whereas GitLab doesn't. Another user says the 1.17 package registry lets them ditch Verdaccio.
Complained about breaking changes in 1.17, such as reserved usernames, and a contested email-validation regex change merged despite objections.
Asked whether Gitea still lacks a good backup and restore mechanism; called this a show stopper for moving to it from Gogs.
